content: Here is the plan for your animation. It differs from what you asked: Changed: the trail draws 100 markers, one every 2 steps, instead of 200; every step still runs. Generate makes it.

proposal.title: Gradient descent: a ball stepping down a loss surface
proposal.description: A curved loss surface with contour lines holds a ball. An arrow on the ball points straight downhill, against the gradient (the slope direction), and a trail marks every position the ball has been. Each step moves the ball a distance set by the learning rate times the slope, in the arrow's direction. You can step one at a time or let it run, drag the ball to a new start, and change the learning rate to see small careful steps, zig-zagging, or overshooting that runs off the surface.

input.request: a ball rolling down a loss surface, step by step

interactions: Take one step: the ball moves once along the downhill arrow and the trail grows by one point
Let the host's play button run the steps continuously, and pause at any time
Drag the ball to any point on the surface to choose a new start; the trail starts again from there
Change the learning rate: small values give many short steps, larger values zig-zag across the narrow bowl, and values above 0.5 on the bowl overshoot and run off the edge
Switch surface to see that the starting point decides which valley the ball ends in
Readouts show the step count, the current loss (height) and the steepness of the slope
notices: Changed: the trail draws 100 markers, one every 2 steps, instead of 200; every step still runs.

proposal.original_request: a ball rolling down a loss surface, step by step
proposal.prompt: A curved loss surface with contour lines holds a ball. An arrow on the ball points straight downhill, against the gradient (the slope direction), and a trail marks every position the ball has been. Each step moves the ball a distance set by the learning rate times the slope, in the arrow's direction. You can step one at a time or let it run, drag the ball to a new start, and change the learning rate to see small careful steps, zig-zagging, or overshooting that runs off the surface.
requirements: Recommended: experiment. Watching each step one at a time, then changing the step size and starting point, shows how gradient descent finds a low point and when it fails.
Interaction: Take one step: the ball moves once along the downhill arrow and the trail grows by one point
Interaction: Let the host's play button run the steps continuously, and pause at any time
Interaction: Drag the ball to any point on the surface to choose a new start; the trail starts again from there
Interaction: Change the learning rate: small values give many short steps, larger values zig-zag across the narrow bowl, and values above 0.5 on the bowl overshoot and run off the edge
Interaction: Switch surface to see that the starting point decides which valley the ball ends in
Interaction: Readouts show the step count, the current loss (height) and the steepness of the slope
Parameter: Learning rate (step size), 0.02 to 0.6, default 0.1
Parameter: Loss surface, one of Stretched bowl (one lowest point), Two valleys (two low points)
Goal: Gradient descent repeatedly steps against the slope. The learning rate controls whether it settles slowly, zig-zags, or overshoots, and the starting point can decide which low point it finds.
assumptions: Illustration: a made-up surface with a simple formula, not a loss from a real trained model.
Each step is plain gradient descent: new position = old position − learning rate × slope, computed exactly from the surface formula.
The bowl is loss = ½(x² + 4y²); it is steeper across than along, which causes zig-zagging. Steps are stable only for learning rates below 0.5.
The two-valley surface is loss = (x² − 1)² + y², with equally low points at x = −1 and x = +1.
Running stops on its own when the slope is almost zero (the ball has settled), when the ball leaves the surface area, or after 200 steps.
The trail draws one marker every 2 steps, at most 100 markers; every step still runs.
limitations: Changed: the trail draws 100 markers, one every 2 steps, instead of 200; every step still runs.
The ball doesn't roll with momentum or speed like a real ball. It jumps from point to point, one gradient step at a time, so it can't coast over a hump.
A single step can go uphill when the learning rate is too large. Loss only falls reliably when the steps are small enough for the surface.
The surfaces have two inputs so they can be drawn. Real models have millions of inputs, and their loss can't be shown as a surface.
